It is these multitudinous associations that give life its colour and its poetry. They are the garnerings of the journey, and unlike material gains they are no burden to our backs and no anxiety to our mind. "The true harvest of my life," said Thoreau, "is something as intangible and indescribable as the tints of morning and evening." It was the summary, the essence, of all his experience. We are like bees foraging in the garden of the world, and hoarding the honey in the hive of memory. And no hoard is like any other hoard that ever was or ever will be. The cuckoo calling over the valley, the blackbird fluting in the low boughs in the evening, the solemn majesty of the Abbey, the life of the streets, the ebb and flow of Father Thames—everything whispers to us some secret that it has for no other ear, and touches a chord of memory that echoes in no other brain. Those deeps within us find only a crude expression in the vehicle of words and actions, and our intercourse with men touches but the surface of ourselves. The rest is "as intangible and indescribable as the tints of morning and evening." It was one of the most companionable of men, William Morris, who said:

That God has made each one of us as lone As He Himself sits.

That is why, in moments of exaltation, our only refuge is silence, and the world of memory within answers the world of suggestion without.

"And what does the seaweed remind you of?" said one, as I looked up after smelling it. "It reminds me," I said, "of all the seas that wash our shores, and of all the brave sailors who are guarding these seas day and night, while we sit here secure. It reminds me also that I have an article to write, and that its title is 'A Bit of Seaweed.'"

message.content:
It is these countless connections that infuse life with richness and artistry. They represent the treasures accumulated along our paths, and unlike physical possessions, they do not weigh us down or create mental strain. “The true harvest of my life,” Thoreau remarked, “is something as intangible and indescribable as the tints of morning and evening.” This encapsulated the quintessence of his experiences. We resemble bees gathering nectar from the world's garden, storing sweet memories in the hive of our minds. Each collection of memories is unique, unlike any other that has existed or will ever exist. The call of a cuckoo echoing across the valley, the blackbird's song in the lower branches at dusk, the grandeur of the Abbey, the vibrant life of the streets, and the rhythmic flow of the River Thames—all of these elements share secrets with us that are meant for no one else, striking chords of reminiscence that resonate in no other mind.

The depths of our being can only express themselves in a rudimentary manner through words and actions, and our interactions with others often skim the surface of our true selves. The deeper aspects remain “as intangible and indescribable as the tints of morning and evening.” The insightful William Morris once expressed it well when he stated: 

That God has made each one of us as lone As He Himself sits.

In moments of profound reflection, we often find solace in silence, where our internal world responds to the external stimuli around us.

As I inhaled the scent of seaweed, a voice inquired, “And what does the seaweed remind you of?” I replied, “It evokes memories of all the oceans that lap against our shores and of the valiant sailors who diligently protect these waters while we enjoy our safety here. It also reminds me that I have an article to compose, and its title is ‘A Bit of Seaweed.’”
